sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To find a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A),] we need to solve the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}] and express the solution as a linear combination of linearly independent vectors. Those vectors form a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A).]

The given matrix is already in reduced row echelon form. So, the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] corresponds to the following system: [MATH: {x_{1} + 3x_{2} = 0; x_{3} − 4x_{4} = 0; 0 = 0]

Here, [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_3] are basic variables corresponding to the pivot columns ([MATH: 1]st and [MATH: 3]rd) and [MATH: x_2,x_4] are free variables corresponding to the non-pivot columns. Therefore, if [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \textrm{Null}(A),] then

[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; x_{3}; x_{4}]|= [− 3x_{2}; x_{2}; 4x_{4}; x_{4}]; = [− 3x_{2}; x_{2}; 0; 0] + [0; 0; 4x_{4}; x_{4}]; = x_{2}[− 3; 1; 0; 0] + x_{4}[0; 0; 4; 1]]

where [MATH: x_2,x_4\in\mathbb{R}.] This implies that

[MATH: [− 3; 1; 0; 0]]

is a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A)] since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To find a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A),] we need to solve the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}] and express the solution as a linear combination of linearly independent vectors. Those vectors form a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A).]

Since [MATH: A\sim B,] the equation [MATH: A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}] is equivalent to the equation [MATH: B\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0},] which corresponds to the following system: [MATH: {x_{1} = 0; x_{2} − (1)/(3)x_{3} + (2)/(3)x_{4} = 0]

So, the general solution is [MATH: x_1=0] and [MATH: x_2=\dfrac{1}{3}x_3 - \dfrac{2}{3} x_4] where [MATH: x_3] and [MATH: x_4] are free variables. Therefore, if [MATH: \mathbf{x}\in\textrm{Null}(A),] then

[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; x_{3}; x_{4}]|= [0; (1)/(3)x_{3} − (2)/(3)x_{4}; x_{3}; x_{4}] = x_{3}[0; (1)/(3); 1; 0] + x_{4}[0; − (2)/(3); 0; 1], x_{3}, x_{4} ∈ R.]

This implies that

[MATH: [0; (1)/(3); 1; 0]]

is a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A)] since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we reduce the matrix [MATH: A] to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

[MATH: A|= [1|0|2; 0|1|2; 0|2|5]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + (− 2)R_{2}; ∼[1|0|2; 0|1|2; 0|0|1]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (− 2)R_{3}; ∼[1|0|2; 0|1|0; 0|0|1]|R_{1}|:=R_{1} + (− 2)R_{3}; ∼[1|0|0; 0|1|0; 0|0|1]]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Remember that the null space [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A)] of a matrix [MATH: A] consists of the solutions to the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}.] To find a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A),] we solve the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}] and express the solution as a linear combination of linearly independent vectors. Those vectors form a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A).]

Content:
To illustrate, consider the matrix [MATH: [1|2|2; 2|4|4; 1|3|3]] Computing the reduced row echelon form of [MATH: A,] we get

Content:
[MATH: [1|0|0; 0|1|1; 0|0|0]]

Content:
So, the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}] is equivalent to the system

Content:
[MATH: {x_{1} = 0; x_{2} + x_{3} = 0; 0 = 0]

Content:
where [MATH: \color{blue}x_1] and [MATH: \color{blue}x_2] are basic variables (corresponding to the pivot columns) and [MATH: \color{red}x_3] is a free variable (corresponding to the non-pivot column).

Content:
Therefore, any vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] in [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A)] has the form

Content:
[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; x_{3}]]

Content:
So, the set [MATH: [0; − 1; 1]] is a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A)] since it is a linearly independent set and the vector [MATH: [0; − 1; 1]] generates the null space of [MATH: A.]

Content:
Note: It might be the case that [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A)] for a particular matrix [MATH: A] equals the so-called zero subspace [MATH: \{ \mathbf{0} \}] containing only the zero-vector. The basis of [MATH: \{ \mathbf{0} \}] is said to be the empty set, which is a set that does not contain any vectors. The empty set is denoted by [MATH: \emptyset] or [MATH: \{\,\}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding a Basis for a Given Null Space

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: [3x_{3} − x_{4}; 4x_{3}; x_{3}; x_{4}]] find a basis for [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Any vector in [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A)] has the form

[MATH: [3x_{3} − x_{4}; 4x_{3}; x_{3}; x_{4}]]

Expanding, we get

[MATH: [3x_{3} − x_{4}; 4x_{3}; x_{3}; x_{4}]|= [3x_{3}; 4x_{3}; x_{3}; 0] + [− x_{4}; 0; 0; x_{4}]; = x_{3}[3; 4; 1; 0] + x_{4}[− 1; 0; 0; 1].]

Therefore, a basis for [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A)] is

[MATH: [3; 4; 1; 0]]

since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A).]

Item 5 — Example: Finding a Basis for the Null Space of a Matrix Given in Reduced Row Echelon Form

Example Prompt:
Find a basis of the null space of the matrix [MATH: [1|3|0|0; 0|0|1|− 4; 0|0|0|0]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A),] we need to solve the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}] and express the solution as a linear combination of linearly independent vectors. Those vectors form a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A).]

The given matrix is already in reduced row echelon form. So, the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] corresponds to the following system:
[MATH: {x_{1} + 3x_{2} = 0; x_{3} − 4x_{4} = 0; 0 = 0]

Here, [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_3] are basic variables corresponding to the pivot columns ([MATH: 1]st and [MATH: 3]rd) and [MATH: x_2,x_4] are free variables corresponding to the non-pivot columns. Therefore, if [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \textrm{Null}(A),] then

[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; x_{3}; x_{4}]|= [− 3x_{2}; x_{2}; 4x_{4}; x_{4}]; = [− 3x_{2}; x_{2}; 0; 0] + [0; 0; 4x_{4}; x_{4}]; = x_{2}[− 3; 1; 0; 0] + x_{4}[0; 0; 4; 1]]

where [MATH: x_2,x_4\in\mathbb{R}.] This implies that

[MATH: [− 3; 1; 0; 0]]

is a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A)] since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A).]

Item 8 — Example: Finding a Basis of the Null Space of a Matrix Given a Row Equivalent Matrix

Example Prompt:
The matrices [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are given below. If [MATH: A] is row equivalent to [MATH: B], then find a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A).]

[MATH: [− 9|3|− 1|2; 1|3|− 1|2; − 5|9|− 3|6]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A),] we need to solve the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}] and express the solution as a linear combination of linearly independent vectors. Those vectors form a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A).]

Since [MATH: A\sim B,] the equation [MATH: A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}] is equivalent to the equation [MATH: B\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0},] which corresponds to the following system:
[MATH: {x_{1} = 0; x_{2} − (1)/(3)x_{3} + (2)/(3)x_{4} = 0]

So, the general solution is [MATH: x_1=0] and [MATH: x_2=\dfrac{1}{3}x_3 - \dfrac{2}{3} x_4] where [MATH: x_3] and [MATH: x_4] are free variables. Therefore, if [MATH: \mathbf{x}\in\textrm{Null}(A),] then

[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; x_{3}; x_{4}]|= [0; (1)/(3)x_{3} − (2)/(3)x_{4}; x_{3}; x_{4}] = x_{3}[0; (1)/(3); 1; 0] + x_{4}[0; − (2)/(3); 0; 1], x_{3}, x_{4} ∈ R.]

This implies that

[MATH: [0; (1)/(3); 1; 0]]

is a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A)] since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate [MATH: \textrm{Null}(A).]
